claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins are highly abundant, ubiquitous, mammalian proteins that line the lysosome limiting membrane.
source: LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins are highly abundant, ubiquitous, mammalian proteins that line the lysosome limiting membrane, and protect it from lysosomal hydrolase action.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established characteristic of LAMP proteins.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 protect the lysosome limiting membrane from lysosomal hydrolase action.
source: LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins are highly abundant, ubiquitous, mammalian proteins that line the lysosome limiting membrane, and protect it from lysosomal hydrolase action.
evidence: This protective function is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to previous work in the introduction.

claim: LAMP2 deficiency causes Danon's disease, an X-linked hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
source: LAMP2 deficiency causes Danon's disease, an X-linked hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: LAMP2 is needed for chaperone-mediated autophagy.
source: LAMP2 is needed for chaperone-mediated autophagy, and its expression improves tissue function in models of aging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Cuervo and Dice, 1996, 2000; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008).

claim: LAMP2 expression improves tissue function in models of aging.
source: LAMP2 is needed for chaperone-mediated autophagy, and its expression improves tissue function in models of aging.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Human LAMP1 and LAMP2 bind cholesterol in a manner that buries the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl group.
source: We show here that human LAMP1 and LAMP2 bind cholesterol in a manner that buries the cholesterol 3β-hydroxyl group
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, including competition experiments with epicholesterol and cholesterol sulfate.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 bind tightly to NPC1 and NPC2 proteins.
source: they also bind tightly to NPC1 and NPC2 proteins that export cholesterol from lysosomes.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4) and microscale thermophoresis experiments (Figure 5) showing direct binding.

claim: NPC1 and NPC2 proteins export cholesterol from lysosomes.
source: they also bind tightly to NPC1 and NPC2 proteins that export cholesterol from lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations (Kwon et al., 2009; Rosenbaum and Maxfield, 2011).

claim: LAMP proteins represent a significant cholesterol binding site at the lysosome limiting membrane.
source: Quantitation of cellular LAMP2 and NPC1 protein levels suggest that LAMP proteins represent a significant cholesterol binding site at the lysosome limiting membrane, and may signal cholesterol availability.
evidence: This is supported by quantitation data showing ~7 × 10^6 LAMP2 molecules per HeLa cell, representing 0.3 mM binding sites in lysosomes.

claim: LAMP proteins may signal cholesterol availability.
source: Quantitation of cellular LAMP2 and NPC1 protein levels suggest that LAMP proteins represent a significant cholesterol binding site at the lysosome limiting membrane, and may signal cholesterol availability.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility based on the abundance and cholesterol-binding capacity of LAMP proteins.

claim: The ability of human LAMP2 to facilitate cholesterol export from lysosomes relies on its ability to bind cholesterol directly.
source: Functional rescue experiments show that the ability of human LAMP2 to facilitate cholesterol export from lysosomes relies on its ability to bind cholesterol directly.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments (Figure 6D) showing that LAMP2 domain 1 I111A/V114A mutant, which cannot bind cholesterol, fails to rescue cholesterol export.

claim: Soluble, purified LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins bind 3H-cholesterol saturably.
source: Soluble, purified, LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins appeared to bind 3H-cholesterol saturably, at a stoichiometry comparable to equimolar amounts of purified, NPC1 N-terminal domain (NTD) that contains a single cholesterol binding site (Infante et al., 2008; Kwon et al., 2009; Figure 1B,D,E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, D, and E.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 bind cholesterol at a stoichiometry comparable to equimolar amounts of purified NPC1 N-terminal domain.
source: Soluble, purified, LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins appeared to bind 3H-cholesterol saturably, at a stoichiometry comparable to equimolar amounts of purified, NPC1 N-terminal domain (NTD) that contains a single cholesterol binding site (Infante et al., 2008; Kwon et al., 2009; Figure 1B,D,E)
evidence: This is shown by comparing binding curves in Figure 1D and E.

claim: NPC1 N-terminal domain contains a single cholesterol binding site.
source: Soluble, purified, LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins appeared to bind 3H-cholesterol saturably, at a stoichiometry comparable to equimolar amounts of purified, NPC1 N-terminal domain (NTD) that contains a single cholesterol binding site (Infante et al., 2008; Kwon et al., 2009; Figure 1B,D,E)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Infante et al., 2008 and Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: Cholesterol binding to LAMP2 is not especially sensitive to pH.
source: Binding was not especially sensitive to pH (Figure 1H) and was complete after ~2 hr at 4°C (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1H.

claim: Cholesterol binding to LAMP2 is complete after approximately 2 hours at 4°C.
source: Binding was not especially sensitive to pH (Figure 1H) and was complete after ~2 hr at 4°C (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown by kinetic data in Figure 1I.

claim: 3H-cholesterol binding to LAMP2 is competed by unlabeled cholesterol.
source: Preliminary experiments showed that 3H-cholesterol binding was competed by unlabeled cholesterol, 24-hydroxycholesterol, but not cholesterol sulfate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 1G.

claim: 3H-cholesterol binding to LAMP2 is competed by 24-hydroxycholesterol.
source: Preliminary experiments showed that 3H-cholesterol binding was competed by unlabeled cholesterol, 24-hydroxycholesterol, but not cholesterol sulfate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 1G.

claim: 3H-cholesterol binding to LAMP2 is not competed by cholesterol sulfate.
source: Preliminary experiments showed that 3H-cholesterol binding was competed by unlabeled cholesterol, 24-hydroxycholesterol, but not cholesterol sulfate (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 1G and Figure 2A.

claim: LAMP2 cholesterol binding occurs via the 3β-hydroxyl moiety of the cholesterol molecule, similar to the orientation with which the NPC1 N-terminal domain binds cholesterol.
source: This suggested that binding occurs via the 3β-hydroxyl moiety of the cholesterol molecule, similar to the orientation with which the NPC1 N-terminal domain binds cholesterol (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from competition experiments with cholesterol sulfate and epicholesterol, and supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: LAMP2 binds 3H-25-hydroxycholesterol with similar apparent affinity as cholesterol.
source: Consistent with this, LAMP2 also bound 3H-25-hydroxycholesterol with similar apparent affinity as cholesterol; binding was competed by excess cold 25-hydroxycholesterol (Figure 1C), as would be expected for a specific interaction.
evidence: This is shown by binding data in Figure 1C.

claim: LAMP2 binding to 3H-25-hydroxycholesterol is competed by excess cold 25-hydroxycholesterol.
source: Consistent with this, LAMP2 also bound 3H-25-hydroxycholesterol with similar apparent affinity as cholesterol; binding was competed by excess cold 25-hydroxycholesterol (Figure 1C), as would be expected for a specific interaction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 25-hydroxycholesterol competes with 3H-cholesterol for binding to LAMP2 protein.
source: More detailed analysis confirmed that 25-hydroxycholesterol (Figure 2B) and 7-ketocholesterol (Figure 2D), but not cholesterol sulfate (Figure 2A), compete with 3H-cholesterol for binding to LAMP2 protein.
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 2B.

claim: 7-ketocholesterol competes with 3H-cholesterol for binding to LAMP2 protein.
source: More detailed analysis confirmed that 25-hydroxycholesterol (Figure 2B) and 7-ketocholesterol (Figure 2D), but not cholesterol sulfate (Figure 2A), compete with 3H-cholesterol for binding to LAMP2 protein.
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 2D.

claim: Epicholesterol failed to compete for cholesterol binding to LAMP2 protein under conditions where cholesterol competed for binding.
source: Epicholesterol is a cholesterol epimer that differs only in the chirality of carbon 3 such that the hydroxyl group is in the alpha rather than beta conformation. Importantly, epicholesterol failed to compete for cholesterol binding to LAMP2 protein under conditions where cholesterol competed for binding (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by competition data in Figure 2C.

claim: Epicholesterol is a cholesterol epimer that differs only in the chirality of carbon 3 such that the hydroxyl group is in the alpha rather than beta conformation.
source: Epicholesterol is a cholesterol epimer that differs only in the chirality of carbon 3 such that the hydroxyl group is in the alpha rather than beta conformation.
evidence: This is stated as chemical knowledge.

claim: The LAMP protein family includes LAMP1, LAMP2, DC-LAMP, BAD-LAMP and Macrosialin.
source: The LAMP protein family includes LAMP1, LAMP2, DC-LAMP, BAD-LAMP and Macrosialin (Wilke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Wilke et al., 2012.

claim: Each LAMP family protein contains a related 'LAMP' domain.
source: Each of these proteins contains a related 'LAMP' domain; LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins each contain two (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as structural knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins each contain two LAMP domains.
source: Each of these proteins contains a related 'LAMP' domain; LAMP1 and LAMP2 proteins each contain two (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal domain 1 of LAMP2 binds more cholesterol than its membrane proximal domain 2 counterpart.
source: Soluble versions of the individual, membrane distal ('domain 1') and membrane proximal ('domain 2') LAMP domains of LAMP2 (Figure 1A) bound cholesterol with different capacity: the N-terminal, domain 1 bound more cholesterol than its membrane proximal, domain 2 counterpart under these conditions (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1F.

claim: Both LAMP2 domains are capable of binding cholesterol within the full length molecule.
source: It is possible that both are capable of binding cholesterol within the full length molecule, as total domain 1 binding was less than that seen with the full length, secreted LAMP2 construct (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that domain 1 alone binds less cholesterol than full-length LAMP2.

claim: LAMP2 purified from cell secretions carries primarily bound cholesterol.
source: Mass spectrometry of the eluted material (Figure 3B) confirmed a profile identical with purified cholesterol standard (Figure 3A) (Figure 3C). These experiments show that LAMP2 purified from cell secretions carries primarily, bound cholesterol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by thin layer chromatography and mass spectrometry data in Figure 3.

claim: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 co-immunoprecipitates with full length NPC1-GFP.
source: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 co-immuno-precipitated with full length NPC1-GFP but not with the control protein, GFP (Figure 4A) or the lysosomal membrane protein, MCOLN1 (Figure 4D), upon expression in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 does not co-immunoprecipitate with GFP control protein.
source: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 co-immuno-precipitated with full length NPC1-GFP but not with the control protein, GFP (Figure 4A) or the lysosomal membrane protein, MCOLN1 (Figure 4D), upon expression in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 does not co-immunoprecipitate with the lysosomal membrane protein MCOLN1.
source: Membrane anchored, endogenous LAMP2 co-immuno-precipitated with full length NPC1-GFP but not with the control protein, GFP (Figure 4A) or the lysosomal membrane protein, MCOLN1 (Figure 4D), upon expression in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of LAMP2 with NPC1 decreases in cells treated for 24 hr with cyclodextrin to remove cholesterol from lysosomes.
source: Interestingly, co-immunoprecipitation decreased in cells treated for 24 hr with cyclodextrin to remove cholesterol from lysosomes (Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009; Rosenbaum et al., 2010) and the plasma membrane (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Cyclodextrin treatment removes cholesterol from lysosomes and the plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, co-immunoprecipitation decreased in cells treated for 24 hr with cyclodextrin to remove cholesterol from lysosomes (Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009; Rosenbaum et al., 2010) and the plasma membrane (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Abi-Mosleh et al., 2009 and Rosenbaum et al., 2010.

claim: Approximately 0.1% cyclodextrin treatment is non-toxic.
source: These conditions (~0.1% cyclodextrin) have been shown to be non-toxic (cf. Ulloth et al., 2007) and did not alter cell growth rate or viability in our hands.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Ulloth et al., 2007 and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claim: Purified, soluble LAMP2 protein binds very tightly to the N-terminal domain of NPC1 protein with a KD of 6 nM.
source: Purified, soluble LAMP2 protein also bound very tightly (and directly) to the N-terminal domain of NPC1 protein (Figure 5A, red) in the presence (or absence, not shown) of cholesterol (KD = 6 nM), as monitored by microscale thermophoresis using AF647 dye-conjugated NPC1 protein—binding significantly altered the fluorescence of NPC1 protein (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by microscale thermophoresis data in Figure 5C.

claim: LAMP2 binding to NPC1 N-terminal domain occurs in the presence or absence of cholesterol.
source: Purified, soluble LAMP2 protein also bound very tightly (and directly) to the N-terminal domain of NPC1 protein (Figure 5A, red) in the presence (or absence, not shown) of cholesterol (KD = 6 nM), as monitored by microscale thermophoresis using AF647 dye-conjugated NPC1 protein—binding significantly altered the fluorescence of NPC1 protein (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations.

claim: No interaction was observed between LAMP2 and the control glycoprotein RNase B.
source: No interaction was observed for the control glycoprotein, RNase B (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown by microscale thermophoresis data in Figure 5E.

claim: NPC2 protein binds to LAMP2 with a KD of 122 nM.
source: The smaller, NPC2 protein (Figure 5B) also bound to LAMP2 (KD = 122 nM), but ~20 fold less tightly that NPC1 N-terminal domain (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is shown by microscale thermophoresis data in Figure 5D.

claim: NPC2 binds to LAMP2 approximately 20 fold less tightly than NPC1 N-terminal domain.
source: The smaller, NPC2 protein (Figure 5B) also bound to LAMP2 (KD = 122 nM), but ~20 fold less tightly that NPC1 N-terminal domain (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is calculated from the KD values: 122 nM for NPC2 vs 6 nM for NPC1 NTD.

claim: NPC2 binding to LAMP2 was monitored in the presence of cholesterol sulfate which occupies the binding site of NPC2 but not LAMP2.
source: binding was monitored in the presence of cholesterol sulfate which will occupy the binding site of NPC2 but not LAMP2 (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental data showing LAMP2 does not bind cholesterol sulfate.

claim: No binding was observed between NPC2 and the control RNase B protein.
source: No binding was seen for NPC2 to the control RNase B protein (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown by microscale thermophoresis data in Figure 5F.

claim: LAMP2 binds directly to both NPC1 N-terminal domain and NPC2 proteins.
source: Thus, LAMP2 binds directly to both NPC1 N-terminal domain and NPC2 proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the microscale thermophoresis experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cholesterol occupancy of NPC1's N-terminal domain does not influence LAMP2 binding in solution.
source: For NPC1, the enhanced binding seen in cells in the presence of cholesterol does not appear to reflect occupancy of NPC1's N-terminal domain, as this variable did not influence LAMP2 binding in solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LAMP2 binds NPC1 NTD equally well in the presence or absence of cholesterol.

claim: NPC1 likely binds cholesterol within its membrane spanning region which may influence its overall conformation.
source: However, it is important to note that NPC1 also likely binds cholesterol within its membrane spanning region which may also influence its overall conformation (Lu et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as knowledge from the literature with citations to Lu et al., 2015 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: HeLa cells contain 6.8 × 10^6 LAMP2 molecules per cell.
source: Using the polypeptide molecular weights and cellular protein determinations, we estimate that HeLa cells contain 6.8 × 106 LAMP2 molecules per cell and 3.7 × 105 NPC1 molecules per cell, or 18 fold more LAMP2 than NPC1
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HeLa cells contain 3.7 × 10^5 NPC1 molecules per cell.
source: Using the polypeptide molecular weights and cellular protein determinations, we estimate that HeLa cells contain 6.8 × 106 LAMP2 molecules per cell and 3.7 × 105 NPC1 molecules per cell, or 18 fold more LAMP2 than NPC1
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HeLa cells contain 18 fold more LAMP2 than NPC1.
source: Using the polypeptide molecular weights and cellular protein determinations, we estimate that HeLa cells contain 6.8 × 106 LAMP2 molecules per cell and 3.7 × 105 NPC1 molecules per cell, or 18 fold more LAMP2 than NPC1
evidence: This is calculated from the absolute molecule counts.

claim: HEK293T cells contain 2 × 10^6 LAMP2 molecules per cell.
source: HEK293T cells contain 2 × 106 LAMP2 molcules per cell and 5.9 × 105 NPC1 molecules (3.6 × fold more LAMP2).
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HEK293T cells contain 5.9 × 10^5 NPC1 molecules per cell.
source: HEK293T cells contain 2 × 106 LAMP2 molcules per cell and 5.9 × 105 NPC1 molecules (3.6 × fold more LAMP2).
evidence: This is calculated from quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HEK293T cells contain 3.6 fold more LAMP2 than NPC1.
source: HEK293T cells contain 2 × 106 LAMP2 molcules per cell and 5.9 × 105 NPC1 molecules (3.6 × fold more LAMP2).
evidence: This is calculated from the absolute molecule counts.

claim: Baby hamster kidney cells contain an absolute volume of approximately 37 µm³ lysosomes and prelysosomes per cell.
source: Baby hamster kidney cells have been estimated to contain an absolute volume of ~37 µm3 lysosomes and prelysosomes per cell (3.7 × 10–14 l) and a lysosome membrane area of 370 µm2 (Griffiths et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Griffiths et al., 1989.

claim: Baby hamster kidney cells contain a lysosome membrane area of 370 µm².
source: Baby hamster kidney cells have been estimated to contain an absolute volume of ~37 µm3 lysosomes and prelysosomes per cell (3.7 × 10–14 l) and a lysosome membrane area of 370 µm2 (Griffiths et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Griffiths et al., 1989.

claim: LAMP2 membrane density in HeLa cell lysosomes is 18,378 molecules per µm².
source: Assuming similar values for HeLa cells, this would represent a LAMP2 membrane density of 18,378 or 5676 molecules per µm2 in HeLa or 293T cell lysosomes, respectively, consistent with previous reports (Granger et al., 1990).
evidence: This is calculated from the total LAMP2 molecules per cell divided by the estimated lysosome membrane area.

claim: LAMP2 membrane density in 293T cell lysosomes is 5,676 molecules per µm².
source: Assuming similar values for HeLa cells, this would represent a LAMP2 membrane density of 18,378 or 5676 molecules per µm2 in HeLa or 293T cell lysosomes, respectively, consistent with previous reports (Granger et al., 1990).
evidence: This is calculated from the total LAMP2 molecules per cell divided by the estimated lysosome membrane area.

claim: Tightly packed viral spike glycoproteins occur at a density of 22,000 molecules per µm².
source: For comparison, tightly packed viral spike glycoproteins occur at a density of 22,000 molecules per µm2 (Quinn et al., 1984).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Quinn et al., 1984.

claim: HeLa cell lysosomes contain 0.3 mM LAMP2-associated cholesterol binding sites.
source: In terms of concentrations, 37 femtoliters of lysosome volume would contain 0.3 mM LAMP2-associated cholesterol binding sites in HeLa cell lysosomes (assuming one mole cholesterol bound per more LAMP2).
evidence: This is calculated from the number of LAMP2 molecules and the lysosome volume.

claim: An individual LAMP domain from DC-LAMP protein is comprised of a novel, beta-prism fold that appears to contain a hydrophobic pocket.
source: The structure of an individual LAMP domain from DC-LAMP protein is comprised of a novel, beta-prism fold that appears to contain a hydrophobic pocket (Wilke et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge with citation to Wilke et al., 2012.

claim: A soluble LAMP2 domain 1-I111A/V114A construct binds significantly less cholesterol than its wild type counterpart.
source: Site directed mutagenesis of hydrophobic residues predicted to line the walls of this cavity yielded purified LAMP2 proteins with impaired cholesterol binding activity. Thus, a soluble, LAMP2 domain 1-I111A/V114A construct yielded a secreted protein (Figure 6B inset, right lane) that bound significantly less cholesterol than its wild type counterpart (Figure 6B inset, left lane and panel B).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Residues I111 and V114 facing the predicted prism fold pocket are important for cholesterol binding.
source: These experiments show that residues facing the predicted, prism fold pocket are important for cholesterol binding and likely contribute to the cholesterol binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing I111A/V114A mutation impairs cholesterol binding.

claim: Full length, wild type LAMP2 rescues cholesterol export in LAMP1/2-deficient MEF cells.
source: Figure 6D shows that as expected, full length, wild type LAMP2 rescued cholesterol export in LAMP1/2-deficient MEF cells
evidence: This is shown by cholesteryl oleate synthesis data in Figure 6D.

claim: Membrane anchored LAMP2 domain 1 shows a level of rescue consistent with its lower capacity for cholesterol binding.
source: membrane anchored LAMP2 domain 1 showed a level of rescue consistent with its lower capacity for cholesterol binding (cf. Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown by cholesteryl oleate synthesis data in Figure 6D and compared to cholesterol binding data in Figure 1F.

claim: Membrane anchored LAMP2 domain 1 I111A/V114A fails to rescue cholesterol export from lysosomes.
source: Importantly, membrane anchored, LAMP2 domain 1 I111A/V114A failed to rescue cholesterol export from lysosomes (Figure 6D), consistent with its inability to bind cholesterol
evidence: This is shown by cholesteryl oleate synthesis data in Figure 6D.

claim: LAMP2's ability to bind cholesterol correlates with its ability to support cholesterol export from LAMP-deficient MEF cells.
source: These experiments demonstrate a direct role for LAMP2 in cholesterol export from lysosomes, and confirm that LAMP2's ability to bind cholesterol correlates with its ability to support cholesterol export from LAMP-deficient MEF cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiments showing that cholesterol-binding mutants fail to rescue cholesterol export.

claim: LAMP proteins facilitate cholesterol export from lysosomes.
source: In addition, LAMP proteins bind tightly to NPC proteins in vitro and in cells, and appear to facilitate cholesterol export from lysosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of binding data and functional rescue experiments.

claim: A recent cellular mass spectrometry analysis estimated LAMP proteins to be present at 260,000 copies per HeLa cell.
source: A recent cellular mass spectrometry analysis (Itzhak et al., 2016) estimated LAMP proteins to be present at 260,000 copies and NPC1 at 29,193 copies per HeLa cell.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Itzhak et al., 2016.

claim: A recent cellular mass spectrometry analysis estimated NPC1 to be present at 29,193 copies per HeLa cell.
source: A recent cellular mass spectrometry analysis (Itzhak et al., 2016) estimated LAMP proteins to be present at 260,000 copies and NPC1 at 29,193 copies per HeLa cell.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Itzhak et al., 2016.

claim: The relative abundance of LAMP proteins to NPC1 matches between this study and the Itzhak et al. 2016 study, but the total levels were 25 fold lower in that study.
source: While the relative abundance of these proteins matches the values we report here, their total level was 25 fold lower in that study.
evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' quantitation and the Itzhak et al. 2016 study.

claim: Transmembrane glycoproteins may be under-represented in mass spectrometry studies due to their unusual protease resistance as proteins of the lysosome membrane.
source: It is possible that these transmembrane glycoproteins were under-represented in due to their unusual protease resistance as proteins of the lysosome membrane, differences in cell confluency and/or differences in HeLa cell lines employed.
evidence: This is offered as a possible explanation for the discrepancy in absolute protein levels.

claim: Lysosomes sense and signal amino acid availability to influence lysosome biogenesis in relation to cellular need.
source: Lysosomes have recently been shown to sense and signal amino acid availability to influence lysosome biogenesis in relation to cellular need (Settembre et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Settembre et al., 2013.

claim: LAMP oligomerization has been reported to correlate with chaperone mediated autophagy.
source: and LAMP oligomerization has been reported to correlate with chaperone mediated autophagy (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Bandyopadhyay et al., 2008.

claim: Cholesterol levels may influence LAMP protein conformation or interaction with other partners to signal the availability of endocytosed cholesterol.
source: Cholesterol levels may influence LAMP protein conformation or interaction with other partners to signal the availability of endocytosed cholesterol to influence autophagy and cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility based on the findings.

claim: The ten fold higher abundance of LAMP proteins compared with NPC1 protein in HeLa cells suggests that LAMP proteins may do more than just facilitate NPC1 function in cholesterol export.
source: The ten fold higher abundance of LAMP proteins compared with NPC1 protein in HeLa cells suggests that LAMP proteins may do more than just facilitate NPC1 function in cholesterol export.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitation data showing LAMP proteins are much more abundant than NPC1.

claim: LAMP2 binds tightly to the N-terminal domain of NPC1 and binds cholesterol with the same orientation as that domain.
source: We have shown that LAMP2 binds tightly to the N-terminal domain of NPC1 and also binds cholesterol with the same orientation as that domain.
evidence: This is concluded from the binding studies and competition experiments with epicholesterol.

claim: Current models suggest that the soluble NPC2 protein binds cholesterol from the internal membranes of lysosomes and delivers it to NPC1 at the limiting membrane.
source: Current models suggest that the soluble NPC2 protein binds cholesterol from the internal membranes of lysosomes and delivers it to NPC1 at the limiting membrane of this compartment (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as an established model with citation to Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: NPC2 can deliver cholesterol to both NPC1 and to LAMP2.
source: One possibility is that NPC2 can deliver cholesterol to both NPC1 and to LAMP2, which is more abundant.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative model based on the findings.

claim: LAMP2 and NPC1 N-terminal domains bind cholesterol in the same orientation.
source: Because LAMP2 and NPC1 N-terminal domains bind cholesterol in the same orientation, it makes sense that NPC2 (which binds in opposite orientation, [Xu et al., 2007]) could transfer the cholesterol between these two proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition experiments and comparison with known NPC1 and NPC2 binding modes.

claim: NPC2 binds cholesterol in opposite orientation to LAMP2 and NPC1 N-terminal domain.
source: Because LAMP2 and NPC1 N-terminal domains bind cholesterol in the same orientation, it makes sense that NPC2 (which binds in opposite orientation, [Xu et al., 2007]) could transfer the cholesterol between these two proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Xu et al., 2007.

claim: The crystal structure of NPC2 bound to the middle lumenal domain of NPC1 supports a direct handoff between NPC1 and NPC2.
source: The recent crystal structure of NPC2 bound to the middle, lumenal domain of NPC1 (Li et al., 2016) supports a direct handoff between NPC1 and NPC2 (Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Li et al., 2016 and Kwon et al., 2009.

claim: Eukaryotic lysosomes are acidic, membrane-bound organelles that contain proteases, lipases and nucleases.
source: Eukaryotic lysosomes are acidic, membrane-bound organelles that contain proteases, lipases and nucleases and degrade cellular components to regenerate catabolic precursors for cellular use (Xu and Ren, 2015; Schwake et al., 2013; Saftig and Klumperman, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Lysosomes degrade cellular components to regenerate catabolic precursors for cellular use.
source: Eukaryotic lysosomes are acidic, membrane-bound organelles that contain proteases, lipases and nucleases and degrade cellular components to regenerate catabolic precursors for cellular use (Xu and Ren, 2015; Schwake et al., 2013; Saftig and Klumperman, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Lysosomes are crucial for the degradation of substrates from the cytoplasm, as well as membrane bound compartments derived from the secretory, endocytic, autophagic and phagocytic pathways.
source: Lysosomes are crucial for the degradation of substrates from the cytoplasm, as well as membrane bound compartments derived from the secretory, endocytic, autophagic and phagocytic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The limiting membrane of lysosomes is lined with lysosomal membrane glycoproteins (LAMPs).
source: The limiting membrane of lysosomes is lined with so-called lysosomal membrane glycoproteins (LAMPs) that are comprised of a short cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane span, and a highly, N- and O-glycosylated lumenal domain (Wilke et al., 2012; Kundra and Kornfeld, 1999; Granger et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: LAMPs are comprised of a short cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane span, and a highly N- and O-glycosylated lumenal domain.
source: The limiting membrane of lysosomes is lined with so-called lysosomal membrane glycoproteins (LAMPs) that are comprised of a short cytoplasmic domain, a single transmembrane span, and a highly, N- and O-glycosylated lumenal domain (Wilke et al., 2012; Kundra and Kornfeld, 1999; Granger et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge with citations.

claim: LAMPs have been proposed to serve as a protective barrier to block hydrolase access to the limiting phospholipid bilayer.
source: Because of their abundance and glycan content, LAMPs have been proposed to serve as a protective barrier to block hydrolase access to the limiting phospholipid bilayer.
evidence: This is stated as an established hypothesis.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 are 37% identical.
source: LAMP1 and LAMP2 are 37% identical and may overlap in function
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: LAMP1 and LAMP2 may overlap in function.
source: LAMP1 and LAMP2 are 37% identical and may overlap in function
